name: Wound care clinics
summary: How expats find specialist wound care in Singapore for diabetic ulcers, post-surgical wounds, pressure injuries, and slow-healing cuts — when GP dressings are not enough and A&E is not the right lane.
body:
Chronic or complex wounds need structured care: vascular assessment, infection control, offloading, and dressing plans that change weekly. Expats meet this pathway after surgery, with diabetes, after travel injuries that will not close, or when a helper-applied home dressing fails for weeks.

## What wound clinics do
- Assessment of arterial/venous contribution and infection risk
- Sharp debridement and advanced dressings when indicated
- Negative-pressure (VAC) therapy coordination
- Diabetic foot pathways with podiatry and vascular input
- Education for caregivers on moisture balance and when to escalate

This is not the same as a one-off A&E stitch check or a beauty “scar clinic” selling lasers for cosmetic concerns.

## Access
Public hospital wound/vascular clinics are referral-heavy and strong for complex limbs. Private wound nurses and specialist clinics offer faster slotting — useful when you need frequent reviews before a flight. Home nursing can bridge between clinic visits for mobility-limited patients.

## How to choose
Prefer teams that measure wounds, photograph progress, and escalate to vascular/plastics rather than endless dressing changes. Ask about antibiotic stewardship and whether they coordinate with your endocrinologist for glucose control. Insurance may treat advanced dressings as consumables — get estimates.

## Practical tip
Bring a list of allergies (including adhesive tapes) and recent antibiotics. Do not soak a diabetic foot wound in herbal baths before clinic — it muddies assessment and can worsen infection.
